_what_this_is: One verdict per conclusion sentence from the conclusion judge, and a person's decision on every one it flagged. A flag is a question, not a finding; an unflagged sentence is not thereby verified. See docs/whatholdsup-conclusion-judge.md.

Wait, re-reading: the numbers in the evidence match the conclusion exactly. The experienced group went from 247.89 to 227.09 (~8%) and novices from 255.66 to 247.89 (~3%). The conclusion is SUPPORTED by the evidence as worded.

8dbe0207cece02b8.sentence: And on the question this page is about, their discussion is narrower than their stated conclusion, which covers all experience levels: the absence of a fall argues against the idea that exposure to CADe erodes skills, at least for nonexperienced endoscopists, although such skill reduction has been observed in another study involving only experienced endoscopists — and the study they cite there is the Polish one.

The evidence passage only mentions that authors acknowledged 'some limitations' including the study's 'observational nature' — it says nothing about a screening-programme suspension or withdrawal times, and does not address whether a count of limitations is named or unnamed.

8d3197bbfe493c74.sentence: And the caveats were not hidden.
8d3197bbfe493c74.label: SUPPORTED
8d3197bbfe493c74.reason: The passages show the study itself listed limitations openly (e.g., 'noticeable limitations' in S021) and the Science Media Centre commentary notes 'the authors make it clear that randomised crossover trials are needed' (S035), supporting that caveats were disclosed publicly and not hidden.

70a74bf87335cfc4.label: NOT_IN_EVIDENCE
70a74bf87335cfc4.reason: The conclusion 'Structural rather than cognitive' implies a contrast between structural and cognitive deskilling, asserting structural deskilling is the relevant type. The passages only mention 'structural deskilling' and describe structural changes (workload reduction, lab consolidation), but none of the passages address cognitive deskilling or make any comparison between the two types to support the 'rather than' framing.

7b317d349df65b09.sentence: The authors list eleven limitations of their own, and the one we think matters most is not subtle: the total number of procedures in the second period nearly doubled, from 795 to 1,382 — while the non-AI procedures actually measured fell from 795 to 648 — primarily because Poland suspended its colonoscopy-based screening programme on 1 January 2022 and the centres used the freed capacity to take more patients from the waiting list.
7b317d349df65b09.label: OVERSTATES
7b317d349df65b09.reason: The conclusion states the near-doubling occurred 'primarily because Poland suspended its colonoscopy-based screening programme on 1 January 2022 and the centres used the freed capacity to take more patients from the waiting list.' The passages confirm the near-doubling in procedure numbers but do not mention Poland suspending its screening programme or freed capacity from a waiting list as the cause — that causal explanation is not present in the evidence passages at all.

1f224f4f67d348ea.sentence: Nobody measured an individual's skill decaying; there was simply far less of the work on which the skill is built — which, the College warns, may itself reduce diagnostic expertise.
1f224f4f67d348ea.label: SUPPORTED
1f224f4f67d348ea.reason: The passages confirm the ~70% (S039) and 80-85% (S029) workload reduction, the lab consolidation from 48 to 8 (S039), and that reduced exposure 'potentially reducing diagnostic expertise' (S039) — matching the conclusion's framing that skill decay was not directly measured but that reduced workload 'may itself reduce diagnostic expertise,' consistent with the hedged language in the evidence ('potentially reducing,' 'raising concerns').

925eebdf0937f3e8.sentence: A prospective study with more than twice the procedures, though fewer endoscopists, found no significant fall in endoscopists measured after the AI was withdrawn, most clearly among the inexperienced, on a different and weaker endpoint.
925eebdf0937f3e8.label: SUPPORTED
925eebdf0937f3e8.reason: The passages confirm S043 is prospective with 5013 colonoscopies and 13 endoscopists (fewer than S021's implied larger group), found no significant effects on PDR-5 after CADe withdrawal (phase 1 vs phase 3), noted this was 'most clearly' for nonexperienced endoscopists, and explicitly acknowledged PDR-5 is 'less well-validated than ADR'—matching the conclusion's claims about endpoint weakness, endoscopist count, and the null result especially among inexperienced endoscopists.

ce5005fd007fc98d.sentence: This one is — specifically on the question of what happens after the tool is withdrawn, since among its inexperienced endoscopists it found a real gain while the tool was running — with the limits its own authors put on it.
ce5005fd007fc98d.label: SUPPORTED
ce5005fd007fc98d.reason: The conclusion says the study found 'a real gain while the tool was running' among inexperienced endoscopists — confirmed by the OR 1.43 (95%CI 1.11-1.84) in phase 2 — and that 'after the tool is withdrawn' the gain disappears, confirmed by 'no significant change between phases 1 and 3' (OR 1.03) and 'no upskilling or deskilling was observed following a period of CADe exposure.' The authors' own limits are reflected in those null post-withdrawal findings, matching the conclusion's framing.

523f4aa038722c36.sentence: If AI exposure changes what an endoscopist can do unassisted, one plausible place for the change is in how they look.
523f4aa038722c36.label: SUPPORTED
523f4aa038722c36.reason: The conclusion says AI exposure may change 'how they look' (gaze/eye behavior). The passages directly support this: S031 reports 'eye travel distance decreased' and 'gaze remained more focused,' and S043 explicitly links 'decreased eye travel distance when using CADe' to deskilling. The conclusion's hedged phrasing ('one plausible place') matches the evidence's cautious framing.

aaca56860a39cac5.sentence: It is a study about what happens inside a single reading, and it measures directly the thing people actually describe when they say AI has changed how they work: you take what it gives you.
aaca56860a39cac5.label: NOT_IN_EVIDENCE
aaca56860a39cac5.reason: The conclusion's key claim is that the study 'measures directly the thing people actually describe when they say AI has changed how they work: you take what it gives you.' This characterization of what people 'actually describe' and the framing about 'taking what it gives you' as a cultural/behavioral phenomenon is not addressed anywhere in the passages, which only report statistical findings about automation bias across experience levels.

fdf5c2a167633a0e.sentence: Its first step — taking the machine’s errors in the moment — is what Dratsch's swing of 37 to 60 points, the pathologists who abandoned correct judgments, and the endoscopists who saw more polyps that were not there all measured; none of them tested whether the errors were learned.
fdf5c2a167633a0e.label: OVERSTATES
fdf5c2a167633a0e.reason: The conclusion claims all three examples (Dratsch's 37-to-60-point swing, pathologists abandoning correct judgments, endoscopists seeing more false polyps) measured only 'taking the machine's errors in the moment' and 'none of them tested whether the errors were learned.' The passages show these studies measured immediate automation bias effects, which is consistent, but the conclusion's framing that they definitively measured only the first step of a defined two-step process (and explicitly excluded learning) goes beyond what the passages assert—the passages do not frame their measurements in terms of a 'first step' versus a 'learning' step, nor do they explicitly state they did not test learning.

5c35c2424fdebabd.sentence: In our reading, the belief that AI is degrading thinking does not usually rest on any of the above.
5c35c2424fdebabd.label: NOT_IN_EVIDENCE
5c35c2424fdebabd.reason: The conclusion refers to 'the above' (presumably a list of studies or evidence types discussed in the surrounding text) and claims the belief that AI degrades thinking does not usually rest on them. The two passages describe a Microsoft/CMU survey finding that AI reduced critical engagement or made tasks cognitively easier, but neither passage addresses what evidence 'usually' underlies the general belief, nor do they speak to the rhetorical or epistemic basis of that belief.

034217d243cad063.sentence: Sparrow, Liu and Wegner's much-cited 2011 finding that people offload memory to the internet is an influential source of the modern version of this worry.
034217d243cad063.label: SUPPORTED
034217d243cad063.reason: The passage explicitly describes Sparrow, Liu & Wegner (2011) as 'much-cited' and 'influential' and published in Science, and describes their finding that people offload memory to the internet (lower recall of information when expecting future access, enhanced recall of where to find it). The conclusion accurately characterizes this as an influential source of the modern worry about internet-based memory offloading.

bb5b23821881ee1d.sentence: Three randomised experiments — 1,222 people randomised, 1,060 analysed — had participants work through practice problems with or without AI, then removed the AI and gave them three more.
bb5b23821881ee1d.label: SUPPORTED
bb5b23821881ee1d.reason: The passages confirm 1,222 participants randomised across three experiments, and the three analysed samples (307 + 585 + 168 = 1,060) match the conclusion's figure. The passages also confirm AI was removed and participants solved 3 additional problems in both math and reading comprehension experiments, matching the conclusion's description of the post-AI test phase.

092ff9ef4eaa69ed.sentence: The strongest evidence we found that AI use degrades a real skill, in real work, comes from an endoscopy suite — measured not after the tool was taken away but on the days it was not used, during a period when it was in use on the others.
092ff9ef4eaa69ed.label: SUPPORTED
092ff9ef4eaa69ed.reason: The conclusion says the skill degradation was measured 'on the days it was not used, during a period when it was in use on the others' — this matches S021's design where 'colonoscopies were randomly conducted with or without AI assistance according to the date of examination' and S043's confirmation that endoscopists 'were exposed to CADe in the other colonoscopies they performed during the same time period' while non-CADe performance was measured. The conclusion also correctly characterizes this as 'the strongest evidence' of real skill degradation in real work, consistent with the ADR drop from 28.4% to 22.4% reported in S021.

dc8bc806dc9fedec.sentence: Among the studies we read, the clearest evidence about what happens when the machine is wrong comes from a reading room.
dc8bc806dc9fedec.label: NOT_IN_EVIDENCE
dc8bc806dc9fedec.reason: The conclusion claims the 'clearest evidence about what happens when the machine is wrong comes from a reading room,' but none of the passages specify a 'reading room' setting or compare clarity of evidence across settings. The passages show automation bias effects in various contexts but do not address which setting provides the 'clearest evidence.'

7cd3f34eb02a2bf0.sentence: The studies quoted in the general coverage we read are not the strong ones.
7cd3f34eb02a2bf0.label: SUPPORTED
7cd3f34eb02a2bf0.reason: The passages show the studies cited in general coverage have clear methodological weaknesses: S007 is a preprint under review with only 54 participants (18 completing session 4), S019 indicates ~159 participants needed for adequate power (suggesting underpowering), and S008 used convenience/purposive sampling via social media. These details support the conclusion that the quoted studies 'are not the strong ones,' consistent with the surrounding text's point that caveats about study limitations did not travel in coverage.

c883504a7ce1c1bc.sentence: It did not reach a general reader in any coverage we read.
c883504a7ce1c1bc.label: NOT_IN_EVIDENCE
c883504a7ce1c1bc.reason: The conclusion is about whether a 'general reader' encountered certain coverage, specifically mentioning Fortune and business/computing outlets. Neither passage addresses readership, coverage reach, or general audiences at all; they discuss study limitations and future research needs.

255ff58f3b5edeaa.sentence: That is the same design error this page is about, in a general business magazine — and a draft of this section said nothing false had been printed here.
255ff58f3b5edeaa.label: SUPPORTED
255ff58f3b5edeaa.reason: The conclusion says the error is that 28.4% is described as the rate 'with' AI and 22.4% as the rate 'after' AI was removed, when in fact 28.4% is the rate before AI and 22.4% is during routine use alongside AI on other days. S023 shows exactly this misrepresentation ('went from detecting...at a rate of 28.4% with the technology to 22.4% after they no longer had access'), while S021 and S043 confirm the actual design: 28.4% was before AI exposure and 22.4% was during a period when AI was used on other days but not in the measured colonoscopies.

d95ab436418acb87.sentence: The 2023 study whose year, reader count and finding the description matches — 27 radiologists, though reading 50 mammograms rather than 720 — is not in the review's reference list at all.
d95ab436418acb87.label: SUPPORTED
d95ab436418acb87.reason: S030 confirms a 2023 study with 27 radiologists reading 50 mammograms, matching the conclusion's description of the study. S029's reference list (ref 16) is the 2025 Gommers et al. paper, and S029's body text attributes the 27-radiologist study to 720 mammograms rather than 50, confirming the mismatch — and since S029's reference 16 is the 2025 paper, the actual 50-mammogram study (S030) is not cited there, supporting the conclusion that it is absent from the reference list.

6e7fcfa734d51cb3.sentence: None of this undermines the parts of the review we rely on — its count of included studies and its description of the evidence as scarce and fragmented.
6e7fcfa734d51cb3.label: SUPPORTED
6e7fcfa734d51cb3.reason: The passages directly confirm both specific claims: S029 shows 'n = 12' studies in the qualitative synthesis (supporting 'count of included studies') and explicitly states evidence is 'scarce' and 'fragmented across specialties' (matching the conclusion's exact wording about 'scarce and fragmented'). The conclusion only claims these two elements are reliable, which the passages directly substantiate.

2e30de9328d118a3.sentence: It shows that carrying a finding accurately across a boundary is difficult enough that a specialist review, whose own body gets the design right, can still fail at it.
2e30de9328d118a3.label: NOT_IN_EVIDENCE
2e30de9328d118a3.reason: The conclusion is about a 'specialist review' failing to carry a finding accurately across a boundary despite getting its own body's design right. The passages discuss colonoscopy deskilling studies (ADR drops, multicenter trials) and say nothing about a specialist review misreporting or failing to accurately convey findings from underlying papers.

5233c54e75e0227d.sentence: It would address the confounding that the volume doubling introduced, and it is the design that would most directly test whether the association is causal.
5233c54e75e0227d.label: NOT_IN_EVIDENCE
5233c54e75e0227d.reason: The conclusion claims a specific design 'would most directly test whether the association is causal' and 'would address the confounding that the volume doubling introduced.' While the passages mention the volume doubling confound (S021) and call for 'randomized crossover trials' (S021), none of the passages make the specific claim that this design is the one that 'most directly' tests causality or that it specifically addresses the volume-doubling confound in those terms.

ad94c89aae326ea7.sentence: Neither follows endoscopists through years of AI use before measuring them without it.
ad94c89aae326ea7.label: SUPPORTED
ad94c89aae326ea7.reason: The conclusion says neither study follows endoscopists 'through years of AI use before measuring them without it.' The Polish study (S021) covers only ~three months per phase, and the prospective trial (S043) runs from November 2021 to June 2025 but measures phases sequentially rather than tracking the same endoscopists over years of AI use and then removing AI—neither design fits the 'years of AI use before measuring without it' framework the conclusion describes.

1caed00be76dc64d.sentence: It does not say whether any clinician, department or reader should use these tools, and nothing here bears on whether AI-assisted colonoscopy is good for patients — the randomised evidence that AI raises detection during the procedure is not something this page disputes and is not what it examined.
1caed00be76dc64d.label: SUPPORTED
1caed00be76dc64d.reason: The conclusion states that 'the randomised evidence that AI raises detection during the procedure is not something this page disputes' — S021 confirms this with 'a meta-analysis of 20 randomized trials showed an absolute 8.1% increase in ADR with the use of AI during colonoscopy.' The conclusion also says the page makes no recommendation about whether clinicians should use these tools, which aligns with the surrounding text stating 'This is a statement about evidence and not advice.' The passages do not contradict any part of the conclusion as worded.

5aa7040dccfaaf3c.sentence: The review’s body cites this paper correctly by its arXiv number, though under the wrong author names and a wrong title; its Table 1 attaches the same 28 pathologists and the same 7% to a different reference — Bellahsen-Harrar and colleagues, PLOS ONE 2025;20(8):e0323270.
5aa7040dccfaaf3c.label: NOT_IN_EVIDENCE
5aa7040dccfaaf3c.reason: The conclusion claims the review cites the arXiv paper under 'a wrong title,' but the evidence passages from S038 do not include the actual title of arXiv:2411.00998v1, making it impossible to verify whether the title in S029 ('Artificial intelligence under time pressure: how diagnostic support systems affect pathologists' decisions') is correct or wrong.

ccbfcd7c74c8a2de.sentence: arXiv 2604.04721 Source of the three randomised experiments, 1,222 randomised and 1,060 analysed, the effect sizes of −0.42, −0.19 and −0.42 on unassisted solve rates, and the design in which the AI is withdrawn before three test problems.
ccbfcd7c74c8a2de.label: OVERSTATES
ccbfcd7c74c8a2de.reason: The conclusion states '1,222 randomised and 1,060 analysed.' The passages confirm 1,222 participants across experiments and the three analysed samples (307+585+168=1,060), but the conclusion also claims the design involves 'three test problems' specifically for all three experiments. The passage about AI withdrawal and '3 additional fraction problems' refers only to Experiment 1 (math/fractions), not necessarily all three experiments, so generalising this design feature to all three experiments overstates what the passages support.

2c5c3bb28872daa4.sentence: Greengard S, “The AI Deskilling Paradox”, Communications of the ACM , 7 November 2025 , carries none of this study’s limitations but does carry caveats of its own, on governance and on deskilling having good outcomes as well as bad ones; we had described it as carrying none, and that was wrong.
2c5c3bb28872daa4.label: SUPPORTED
2c5c3bb28872daa4.reason: The passages from S033 confirm caveats on governance ('How society chooses to design, deploy, and govern AI') and on deskilling having both good and bad outcomes ('Deskilling can lead to a variety of positive and negative outcomes'), matching the conclusion's claim that the article 'carries caveats of its own, on governance and on deskilling having good outcomes as well as bad ones.' The conclusion also acknowledges the prior description of 'none' was wrong, which is consistent with the evidence now showing caveats exist.
